newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW-Boetsch wants tough telecoms regulation.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Boetsch wants tough telecoms regulation.

text.p: German Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch said on Tuesday a decision forcing Deutsche Telekom to grant rivals access to its networks was intended to promote competition and set a tough standard.

Speaking to Reuters in his Bonn office after making the ruling, Boetsch said he did not want the government to be seen now as taking a hard line on the former monopoly. Instead, he said he was ensuring that "competition gets underway."

Boetsch ruled in favour of a complaint by new telecoms companies and ordered Deutsche Telekom to provide rivals with an offer for so-called unbundled interconnection by July 14 or face penalty proceedings.

The ruling means Telekom must provide rivals the possibility of directly connecting their networks to the individual customer access lines, or the last mile from the local switch to the home or business, instead of having to go through Telekom's switching service. This will greatly reduce costs for Telekom's rivals and promote competition.
"The last mile was always at the centre of the discussion," he said. "If the last mile cannot be bridged or only with extraordinary costs then, competition will remain a theory."
Deutsche Telekom can appeal the ruling in Administrative Court.
Six months before full competition on European telecoms markets, Boetsch said it was clear more work needed to be done but that main reforms had been implemented.
"It is obvious that we won't be running at full throttle on January 1, 1998, but we are prepared. I am satisfied," he said.

When the telecoms market is opened, the postal ministry will be dissolved and Boetsch will pass on the job of regulating the industry to the still-to-be formed Regulatory Agency. He said he wanted to leave a solid legacy for his successor.

"I am interested in seeing that my relatively good reputation in this matter is maintained," he said. "We have to prove that we are serious about regulation. Otherwise, companies with a dominant position in the market will press others up against the wall."

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet plans to appoint the president of the new Regulatory Agency on Wedesday. Boetsch would not comment on press reports he plans to propose naming Dieter Scheuerle, a senior post ministry official whose possible appointment has been criticised by Telekom rivals.

The Regulatory Council, consisting of parliament and federal state representatives, proposed appointing Peter Landsberg, a former chairman of Alcatel SEL, but the cabinet will make the final decision.

Asked if there were any differences between the Christian Democrats (CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) in the coalition over the appointment, Boetsch said "I presume there will be a unanimous decision in cabinet (on Wednesday)."

He played down reports of tensions between Bonn and Washington that arose when reports surfaced of a secret pact between Boetsch and Finance Minister Theo Waigel over shielding Telekom from competition.
The government hopes to sell a 25-percent stake in Telekom this year, and reports claimed Waigel was worried too much competition lower the share price.
Boetsch said reports were based on misinterpretation of an exchange with Waigel in 1996 over questions the finance ministry had presented concerning the new Telecommunications Act.

"I swear, since then, I haven't exchanged a single word with Waigel about regulatory matters, and the finance ministry has never attempted to exert influence on any regulatory matters," he said. --william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150)
